articles.title_orig: Why China needs more income taxation - Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.title_zh: Why China needs more income taxation - Peterson Institute for International Economics
articles.content_orig:
Authors' note: We thank Zhuowen Li for research assistance.
China's large current account surpluses, reflecting its large trade surpluses, remain a concern around the world. Countries that absorb large quantities of Chinese exports without the ability to sell similar quantities of goods to China fear that China's export orientation threatens their industrial sectors. Weak Chinese domestic demand exacerbates the trade imbalance. Private consumption in China is only 40 percent of GDP, far lower than in most countries. [1]
International imbalances have long been understood by economists to be macroeconomic phenomena. When a country (e.g., the United States) persistently spends more than it earns, it obtains the additional consumption from abroad, running a current account deficit that is financed through international borrowing. When a country (e.g., China) persistently earns more than it spends, it accumulates international assets and runs a current account surplus, shipping excess production abroad.
To address this imbalance and achieve other policy goals described below, China can reform its tax system to encourage more consumption at home. As the country with the world's largest absolute current account surplus, China should rely more on a progressive personal income tax instead of leaning so heavily on consumption taxes. This would be in keeping with its avowed socialist principles while incentivizing domestic spending.
For its part, the United States should expect its trade wars to be ineffective in remedying its trade imbalance, since international imbalances are driven by macroeconomic factors. In recent decades, the United States has emerged as the world's largest debtor. Since 2020, it has accounted for more than half of the world's net current account deficits. Yet the massive US tariffs of 2025–26 have only had modest effects on the US current account. For the United States, reducing fiscal deficits (averaging about 6 percent of GDP of late) would be far more effective in reducing US national dissaving, although there appears to be little political appetite for fiscal restraint at present.
Unlike the United States, China does not have a fiscal situation responsible for its international imbalances. The Chinese government does not run a budget surplus. Instead, it has run large and growing on-budget deficits of more than 5 percent of GDP in recent years, reducing Chinese national savings (figure 1). [2] The Chinese government deficits have not been enough to offset a large excess of private savings over private investment or to lift China's economy convincingly out of deflationary pressures, however. While a larger fiscal deficit isn't called for, China should consider reforming its tax structure, including an expansion of its income tax, to discourage excess private saving.
What accounts for the excess of Chinese savings?
It has roots in the Chinese housing bust, which has sharply curtailed private investment without diminishing China's high private saving rate ( Huang 2026 ). Lower house values—especially without the availability of alternative savings options including international investments—may encourage higher saving, as the housing sector becomes a less reliable source of value and households pursue alternative savings goals.
China's government understandably argues that they have no more room to deficit finance aggregate demand in China. By the end of 2025, general government debt had reached nearly 70 percent of GDP, or nearly 130 percent of GDP when off-budget debt is included ( International Monetary Fund [IMF] 2026 ). Total tax revenue as a share of GDP peaked in 2012 and has fallen steeply since then (figure 2). Beijing's tax and government fee cuts to support the economy since 2018 accelerated this decline. The housing bust that began in 2021 has further prolonged and deepened that trend. If anything, the Chinese government needs to raise taxes, as the population is aging and the principal non-tax source of revenue—land sales by local governments—is unlikely to rebound following the housing sector bust.
Indeed, China has often declared its interest in spurring domestic consumption, but it seems to throw up its hands when it comes to taking steps to reach that goal. But while fiscal balances are limited in their ability to help drive macroeconomic aggregates, the design of China's fiscal policy has an important role to play.
In particular, China should look to reforming its tax structure. Its very weak personal income tax was only about 1.2 percent of GDP in 2025, the lowest share among G20 countries other than Saudi Arabia, which does not impose a personal income tax. By contrast, China's consumption tax burden totaled about 6 percent of GDP in 2025 (including VAT, excise tax, and tariffs). Overall, tax revenue in China is very low for an economy on the cusp of advanced economy status, at only 12.6 percent of GDP in 2025. Including social security contributions, which China classifies as fees rather than taxes, the total tax burden amounted to 20.4 percent of GDP in 2023—higher than only India, Indonesia, Mexico, and Saudi Arabia among G20 countries (figure 3).
Tax reform that more heavily taxes incomes, instead of consumption, could achieve five important aims in China.
First, it could strengthen and modernize China's tax system, making it more suited to the fiscal challenges ahead. There are ample fiscal needs in China, including supporting China's elderly population, responding to disruptions, and pursuing countercyclical fiscal policy when needed. At present, China's fiscal capacity is quite low relative to that of other G20 countries.
Second, by taxing income instead of consumption, China could rectify the tilt in its fiscal system toward consumption over savings. China's biggest tax levers exempt savings from taxation; a broad income tax does not. Chinese government officials often say they want to spur consumption, but the structure of their tax system does the opposite, by leaning on consumption taxes rather than income taxes.
Third, these changes would make China's tax system more progressive, a suitable aim for an economy that is avowedly socialist. When we raised these issues with Chinese government officials in a recent trip to Beijing, we were often told that the Chinese population cannot afford tax increases. We agree that this is the case for many in the population, particularly rural residents and/or those with lower incomes. But the ability to make well-off households pay a higher share of their income in tax is a key attribute of a progressive income tax. An income tax can also easily shelter lower-income citizens from high tax burdens. A well-designed income tax system may even provide negative tax rates (i.e. a tax refund) for households with lower incomes—through earned income tax credits (EITCs)—providing both means tested income support and incentives to work outside the informal sectors of the economy.
In the United States, about 40 percent of households pay no federal income tax, mostly because of their lower incomes. And in China more than 70 percent of the individuals who file income tax declarations end up not paying personal income tax. The 1 percent of tax filers earning more than 1 million RMB (about $150,000) annually account for over half of the total personal income tax collected. [3] As such, China's current personal income tax system is progressive in taxing the highest earners. The challenge for the Chinese government is to maintain that progressivity while expanding the personal income tax base.
A broader, but still progressive, income tax can also help tackle China's regional income disparities. Such a tax would fall more heavily on richer regions, allowing the central government to redistribute fiscal resources to lower income regions. articles.title_orig: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.title_zh: Jim Beam won't resume distilling at flagship Kentucky distillery in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Jim Beam’s decision to temporarily pause operations at its Kentucky distillery on America Reports.
Jim Beam will indefinitely pause production at its historic flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, amid declining whiskey sales and record inventories.
The iconic American whiskey brand, owned by Japanese multinational brewing and distilling company Suntory Global Spirits , announced last December that it would pause production at its Clermont, Kentucky facility for one year, with plans to resume operations in 2027, Food Dive reported.
However, in a new development, it is now uncertain when the Clermont distillery will begin operations again, the company told The Courier Journal.
NEW 123.4-PROOF WHISKEY PROMPTS EXPERT WARNING THAT STRONGER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER
Suntory told the outlet that it manages its Kentucky production in accordance with demand, inventory and long-term needs.
In December 2025, Jim Beam announced a one-year closure of its flagship distillery in Clermont, Kentucky, but announced last week that the facility will remain closed indefinitely as the company assesses production needs. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for NYCWFF and Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
The company noted that it plans to reassess production needs in the future.
In the meantime, Jim Beam has moved production to its nearby Booker Noe Distillery in Boston, Kentucky, which, with an output of 45 million original proof gallons annually, is the brand’s largest distillery, according to Food Dive.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The brand's Fred B. Noe distillery, located on the Clermont facility's campus, will continue its operations producing whiskey labels including Knob Creek, Little Book and Booker's, Inc. reported.
Fox News Digital reached out to Jim Beam and the brand’s parent company, Suntory Holdings, for comment.
Whiskey inventories are at record highs in the U.S. and Kentucky in particular as consumer demand for the spirit continues to decrease. (Bryan Woolston/Getty Images)
Jim Beam’s move comes amid an ongoing decrease in consumer demand for whiskey , with large quantities of the spirit sitting untouched.
Whiskey inventory in the U.S. is three times higher than estimated annual demand, global beverage alcohol data and insight firm IWSR reported in October.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"The unifying theme across Scotch, US, Japanese and Irish whiskey is polarisation by price tier: we are seeing growth narrowing to specific bands within each whisky sub-category, rather than spreading across the price ladder," said Marten Lodewijks, IWSR managing director and president.
Jim Beam's parent company said that it remains unclear when operations will resume at the historic James B. Beam Distilling Co. distillery in Clermont, Kentucky. (Joe Hendrickson/Getty Images)
"And in most cases, that growth is concentrating at the premium end, while the mainstream and value tiers absorb the pain," he added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Members of the Kentucky Distillers Association held an inventory of 16.1 million barrels of whiskey as of October 2025, according to the organization’s website.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Total beverage alcohol sales declined for the third consecutive year in 2025, according to IWSR.
Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits
articles.title_zh: Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits
articles.content_orig:
Professor of Critical Development Studies at the Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, York University, Toronto.
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.
It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.
Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.
The contradiction is built into the negotiating process. Under the Paris Agreement, governments determine their own emissions commitments, with no enforcement mechanism to compel a country to stop expanding fossil-fuel production. COP decisions also depend on consensus, giving determined holdouts considerable leverage. The result is an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do.
That does not mean all countries are equally responsible. Nor does it mean that every COP has achieved nothing. The Paris framework helped establish common goals, and climate summits have encouraged investment and cooperation. Antalya itself adopted limited decisions on other matters, including one on a just transition. But these gains cannot substitute for a credible timetable to wind down fossil-fuel extraction. The distinction matters: diplomatic activity is not the same as structural change.
Indeed, fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall. Producing states defend revenues and geopolitical influence, while consuming states continue to rely on cheap energy and established infrastructure. Even governments that speak forcefully about climate ambition face incentives to protect their own industries and voters from immediate costs. The global energy transition is therefore not simply a technological problem. It is a struggle over who must relinquish assets, profits and power.
This helps explain the appeal of technological promises. The failed Antalya draft promoted carbon-removal technologies to deal with warming beyond 1.5C, while disagreements also centred on carbon capture and storage. Such approaches may have limited roles in reducing or counterbalancing emissions from difficult-to-abate sectors. But when presented as substitutes for reducing extraction, they allow governments and corporations to promise that future machines will repair the damage of continued emissions. The political benefit is immediate; the promised atmospheric benefit remains uncertain.
The same structural inequality shapes climate finance. Countries that contributed least to historical warming face mounting costs from droughts, floods, displacement and adaptation. Yet the proposed $120bn adaptation target disappeared from the revised text and disputes over financial commitments helped sink the talks. Wealthy governments can celebrate climate ambition while leaving poorer countries to borrow, divert public spending or simply absorb losses.
This is precisely why climate finance cannot be treated as discretionary charity. It concerns responsibility for harms produced through an unequal world economy. Grants, predictable funding and meaningful decision-making power for affected countries are not extras to be negotiated after emissions targets. They are conditions of a transition that poorer countries can undertake without sacrificing education, healthcare and basic development.
There is also a danger in allowing the EU to emerge from Antalya as the uncomplicated defender of climate justice. Its refusal to accept a pact silent on fossil fuels was justified. But wealthy countries cannot demand ambitious language abroad while resisting the financial obligations and domestic changes that would give it substance. Conversely, some developing countries depend on fossil-fuel income or need affordable energy. A just phaseout must distinguish their circumstances from those of rich, historically high-emitting economies.
What would a different climate politics look like? It would begin with enforceable plans for ending new fossil-fuel expansion and phasing down production, with richer countries moving first and fastest. It would fund adaptation and loss and damage through reliable, primarily grant-based transfers rather than debt-creating loans. And it would give countries most vulnerable to climate change greater influence over the decisions that determine their futures.
None of this requires abandoning multilateralism. It requires refusing to confuse its survival with success. When consensus rules repeatedly protect the interests most responsible for the crisis, governments must also pursue complementary agreements, domestic regulation and coalitions willing to move faster. Otherwise, the promise of universal participation becomes a mechanism for universal delay.
The collapse of COP31 is a warning, not because climate diplomacy has suddenly stopped working, but because its limits have become impossible to disguise. The world does not lack knowledge of what causes warming. It lacks a political system willing to confront those who benefit from causing it. Until that changes, each summit will be judged by the agreements it produces, while the atmosphere registers the emissions it fails to prevent.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title_orig: The trouble with the middle powers project
articles.title_zh: The trouble with the middle powers project
articles.content_orig:

Middle powers had a middling moment
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for middle power cooperation raised expectations for 2026, but the Asia Power Index shows a mixed picture.
In a speech delivered at the World Economic Forum in January, Mark Carney declared a rupture in the rules-based order, entreating middle powers to act together to forge flexible, issue-based coalitions rather than relying on dominant superpowers. 1 He called on like-minded middle powers, such as Australia, Japan, and South Korea, to seize the initiative and shape the emerging order. However, their performance over the year proved uneven.
Australia’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 31.7 points, but its Economic Relationships score rose. This was driven by gains in Economic Diplomacy, where it climbed three places to fourth, particularly in its economic statecraft. Expert respondents praised Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s ability to advance Australia’s economic interests, reflecting his successful regional visits to secure petroleum and fertiliser supplies in the wake of the Iran war. However, they rated him less effective at advancing Australia’s diplomatic interests in Asia: more than a third of respondents gave lower appraisals than in 2025, pulling his score down 14 points to 76. The fall contributed to a modest decline in Australia’s overall Diplomatic Influence.
Japan’s comprehensive power dipped slightly to 38.6 points. Yet, for the first time in the Index’s history, it improved on all four resource measures, including a first-ever rise in its Economic Capability. Its Cultural Influence also rose, largely on the back of its growth as an education destination. But these gains could not offset a further slide in Economic Relationships, where its score fell 15 per cent to a record low of 31.2. For the first time since the inception of the Index, Japan is not the primary foreign investor in any other Index country, down from three in the previous edition. An $8 billion increase in Chinese investment into Thailand and burgeoning bilateral tech investment between Taiwan and the United States meant Japan lost its status as the top investor in these three countries. As a result, Japan dropped out of the top three economic partners, and Singapore moved ahead. Experts judged Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to be a more effective leader at the global level than her predecessor, Shigeru Ishiba, but rated her regional leadership less highly. Japan’s score on that indicator fell nearly 9 points to its lowest level yet of 81.
South Korea had a difficult 2026. Its comprehensive power score fell to 31 points, with declines in five of the eight measures: Economic and Military Capability, Economic Relationships, Defence Networks, and Diplomatic Influence. Its relationship with a more transactional United States came under strain, with President Trump calling for cuts to combined military exercises. The shakier alliance has weighed on assessments of South Korea’s Military Capability, with experts less confident in its armed forces’ ability to fight a ground war. Compounding this, President Lee Jae Myung is seen as less able to manage President Trump, weakening perceptions of his regional leadership and his ability to advance South Korea’s economic interests. The country’s cultural appeal, however, is as strong as ever, with the long-term growth of K-Pop and K-Dramas complementing its growing reputation as a tourist destination.
That all three countries lost Diplomatic Influence this year calls into question their ability to shape the international system.
While the picture for like-minded middle powers is mixed, Pakistan punched above its weight in 2026, rising 0.6 points to reach a comprehensive power score just above 15 (the threshold for middle powers). Its shuttle diplomacy gave it a brief role in US–Iran ceasefire talks, culminating in the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
Experts rated Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s regional and global leadership much more highly as a result, lifting Pakistan’s Diplomatic Influence 2.8 points to 35.6. However, the Memorandum fell short of its key aim — a final deal to end the conflict — and failed to prevent the renewal of hostilities, which resumed within a month of its signing. Pakistan is unlikely to sustain this score in future editions.
Dr Hunter Marston is the Director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute and Project Lead for the Asia Power Index .
Jack Sato is a Data Analyst for the Asia Power Index at the Lowy Institute.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.title_zh: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday lauded an "exemplary" military operation that sank one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port, after Kyiv's forces struck their target with several domestically made naval drones.
The incident followed a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea on Saturday and occurred less than a week after damage was inflicted on Russian President Vladimir Putin 's prized Crimea bridge.
In a social media post , Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces deployed seven sea drones to attack the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, at Benghazi's port in the early hours of Sunday morning. Ukraine's president posted dramatic video footage showing Ukraine's naval drones triggering a massive explosion on the Russian ship.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It's one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters," he added.
Satellite imagery taken on Sunday showed the Merkury mostly underwater, having capsized
The Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, was hit by Ukrainian forces. A Ka-27 military helicopter on the Merkury was also destroyed.
Asked about reports of attacks on Russian ships off the coast of Libya, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said information on this would be provided via the Defense Ministry.
The Security Service of Ukraine, the SBU, said Monday that the attacks "once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics have no safe routes even far beyond the Black Sea," according to a Google translation.
"Such unique special operations destroy the enemy's logistical capabilities and force Russia to pay for aggression even at a strategic distance from Ukraine," the SBU said via Telegram.
The United Nations Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, expressed "serious concern" over the drone attacks in a statement saying the country "cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts."
"UNSMIL calls for an immediate, independent and transparent investigation to establish the facts and hold those responsible to account," it added.
The incident is not the first time Libya has seen attacks linked to the Russia-Ukraine war near its territory.
In March, Moscow's Transport Ministry accused Ukraine of striking the Arctic Metagaz, a liquefied natural gas tanker, as part of a suspected sea drone attack in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta.

articles.title_orig: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk’s AI company over sexual deepfakes
articles.title_zh: Virginia, Oregon sue Musk’s AI company over sexual deepfakes
articles.content_orig:
Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator.
Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others.
In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content.
Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images.
"This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation."
SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products.
SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California.
In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction.
When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content.
SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions."
The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company.
Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance.
State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms.
In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, powered by the RTX Spark N1X SoC, passed its most difficult test yet last month at the heart of Windows on Arm laptops . Now we get to see how that chip serves as a Windows on Arm foundation for compact desktops.
We’ve got our hands on the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+, a $7,500 RTX Spark mini PC that gives Windows-native creators and local AI trailblazers access to the same powerful 6144-core Blackwell GPU and 20-core Arm CPU that we recently put to the test in the Surface Laptop Ultra , along with a 128GB pool of unified memory and 4TB of storage in our tested config.
We’ve been testing Nvidia GB10-powered desktop systems for almost a year now in the form of the DGX Spark and friends, and the EdgeMesa N AI+’s design is typical of the breed. It’s wrapped in a slightly hollow-feeling matte aluminum shell with shiny diamond-cut edges and a white plastic back plate.
The design and build quality of this system is a tad underwhelming for the price. It feels nice enough, but It’s hardly a precision-milled statement piece for your desk like a Mac Mini or Mac Studio.
The EdgeMesa draws cool air in through its perforated front panel, which then passes through a dual-fan heatsink with a vapor-chamber base and exhausts through the back panel. The rounded rectangle on the top half of the front panel might look like an optical drive tray, but it’s a purely cosmetic accent.
Around back, the EdgeMesa comes equipped with a 10 Gigabit Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB Type-C 20 Gbps ports with DisplayPort Alt Mode support. A fourth USB-C port is dedicated to the system’s 240 W USB-PD power adapter. The EdgeMesa also has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 radios inside.
Even with a wireless keyboard and mouse, three 20Gbps USB-C ports feel a bit skimpy as the sole expansion options on a $7,499 PC that’s positioned as a do-it-all desktop for content creation and gaming. If you need to connect multiple monitors to an RTX Spark via USB-C, those scant options for peripheral connectivity shrink even further.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
For comparison, a similarly priced Mac Studio gives you four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports around back and two more USB Type-C ports, plus an SD card reader, up front. The Mac even provides a headphone jack, while the EdgeMesa requires you to plug in a USB headset or DAC or pair Bluetooth earbuds for audio output.
Even the Mac Mini gives you three Thunderbolt ports out back and two USB 3 10Gbps ports out front.
In use, the tightly spaced, rear-mounted USB-C ports make for an annoying time when doing frequent unplugging and replugging of devices like card readers and external SSDs that are typical in creative workflows. Even one front-panel USB-C port would have made a huge difference in the ease of use of this design.
The EdgeMesa also drops the handy ConnectX RDMA NIC that lets you cluster DGX Spark systems together to run larger AI models. That omission raises a weighty question: is Windows support and application compatibility important enough to trade away any chance of expanding your local AI foundation in the future?
Having tested DGX Sparks for some time now, I’m not sure that’s a wise trade-off, given that most anybody reading this already has a capable Windows PC or Mac that can link up with a DGX Spark for many local AI compute jobs using the Nvidia Sync app.
DGX Spark prices are rising, but you can get MSI's own EdgeXpert with 128GB of memory and a 4TB SSD on sale for $8,099 right now (or $8,499 at full price). Even a $1000 difference in price for that ConnectX NIC in this rarefied air of PC pricing would give me pause if I'm seriously considering how to add local AI capacity to my home.
If you have no inclination whatsoever to learn Linux or networking concepts and just want a no-questions-asked, AI-capable Windows mini PC that can serve as your primary desktop, an RTX Spark system like this may be the way to go. But you'll want to be really sure of your decision before dropping this much cash.
20-core Arm CPU (10 X925 performance cores, 10 A725 efficiency cores)
6144-core (48 SM) Nvidia Blackwell integrated GPU
128GB LPDDR5X, 273 GB/s shared memory bandwidth
10 Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4
3x USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C ports (rear)
The performance of the Nvidia GB10 SoC's CPU and GPU resources, whether under DGX OS or Windows, is well-trodden ground by this point. But for a fresh point of comparison, we grabbed AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo , swapped in a spare SSD, and installed Windows 11 Pro, as the Ryzen AI Halo is the only other Windows-ready platform with a large unified memory pool for AI adventurers.
In the Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark under Windows, the Ryzen AI Halo delivers a slightly higher single-threaded score than the MSI EdgeMesa’s RTX Spark Superchip, but its multithreaded score trails the Nvidia part. Using Linux, we would expect both scores to be higher for the Ryzen CPU. But the broader point remains the same: you can expect similar performance from both of these CPUs under Windows.
We’ve left Apple’s Mac Studio with M4 Max in these charts just to emphasize the large performance lead Apple Silicon holds in this benchmark, even with older chips. The current M5 Max would likely open an even larger lead.
In the AgentPerf-Local AI inference benchmark, the MSI EdgeMesa delivered performance practically identical to Microsoft ’s Surface Laptop Ultra when running the same Qwen 3.8 27B model with DFlash2 speculative decoding. Its desktop form factor doesn’t seem to give it any extra performance headroom, at least for this LLM serving

articles.title_orig: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.title_zh: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
articles.content_orig:
Oxfam in collaboration with the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) has published a new report on how Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival.
Israel's destruction of Gaza through the extensive use of explosive and incendiary weapons has made air, soil and water dangerous to Palestinians now and for decades to come, with indicators of toxic contamination across almost the entirety of the Strip. With international attention increasingly turning to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought, but as a vital undertaking in parallel.
This paper presents a comprehensive picture of Gaza's contamination landscape. Satellite-derived data, remote sensing analysis, and geolocated conflict incident databases are used to spatially map contamination risks across Gaza, drawing on scientific and legal literature to assess exposure pathways, potential health consequences, and the legal implications of environmental harm. It demonstrates that the evidence already available is sufficient to conclude that contamination is widespread, severe and consequential, and that the destruction and contamination of Gaza’s environmental resources and systems raise serious concerns under international humanitarian law (IHL), international human rights law (IHRL) and occupation law.
The research found that that the scale and intensity of the Israeli military’s onslaught has affected approximately 78 per cent of Gaza’s land area, with the report’s spatial analysis identifying indicators of potential contamination across more than 99 per cent of the territory; highlighting the scale and near-total geographical spread of pollution risks.
Oxfam calls for a full, independent, field-based Post-Conflict Environmental Assessment, which is needed to establish what contaminants are present, where they are found and at what concentrations; determine the risks they pose to people and the environment; and identify what needs to be done to address them. The absence of a full, independent, field-based post-conflict environmental assessment is a direct consequence of Israel’s continued refusal of independent access to Gaza.
Israel must end its genocide and siege of Gaza and to allow unrestricted access for aid, environmental assessment and essential equipment. Recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be owned and led by Palestinians themselves. It must be rights-based, reparations-oriented, and rooted in accountability. International funding does not replace Israel’s obligation to make reparations for the harm caused by its unlawful acts.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock jumps as DC makes stunning u-turn on Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock jumps as DC makes stunning u-turn on Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A not-so-subtle shift in tone in the Jensen Huang saga has sent Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock reeling this month.
Washington has gone from wanting Huang out of Nvidia in the wake of his affairs going public to wanting him back in the corner office.
Nvidia stock rose 9% in premarket trading on Monday as President Trump explicitly called on Nvidia's board to rehire its ousted co-founder. He argued that bringing Huang back would be the best thing for the company — and for the United States.
"I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.
Just days ago, Trump was floating former Apple ( AAPL ) CEO Tim Cook as a possible replacement.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also subtly changed his tune on Huang.
After demanding that Nvidia look outside the company for its next CEO, Bessent was asked on "Face the Nation" on Sunday whether Huang could return.
"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent said. That's a clever answer, and a notable retreat from his tougher earlier position.
Odds on Kalshi on Huang returning as CEO have jumped to 16% from under 10% last week.

articles.title_orig: Flights grounded in Belgium due to austerity measures strike
articles.title_zh: Flights grounded in Belgium due to austerity measures strike
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.
"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.
Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.
"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.
One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.
Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.
"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.
The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.
One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.
"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.
The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | LIRR riders sharing phone location get $8 ticket warnings — despite claims of no tracking
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | LIRR riders sharing phone location get $8 ticket warnings — despite claims of no tracking
articles.content_orig:
They’re being tracked on the tracks!
Long Island Rail Road riders sharing their location are getting ticket activation warnings — despite officials’ claims that they wouldn’t monitor geodata to police commuters.
The LIRR hiked prices in January and started issuing a new $8 fine if riders didn’t activate their tickets on the TrainTime app prior to boarding, with the transit agency saying it would only use a “timekeeping function” to check if the rules were being broken.
But The Post found phones sharing their locations received warnings while phones not sharing didn’t receive any warnings — which cybersecurity experts said shows the app may be “abusing user data.”
“The tests [The Post ran] are pretty black and white — they’re clearly using some sort of location data when they say they’re not,” said Harry Maugans, a cybersecurity expert and privacy advocate.
“People should care about this, because if they don’t, one day we’re going to wake up in an Orwellian state,” said Maugans, who is CEO of data privacy firm Privacy Bee.
The Post used two phones with different location settings over multiple trips spanning various dates, with both phones having unactivated tickets at the start of a trip.
One phone, with its location set to “always” sharing, was consistently hit with pop-up late-activation warnings early in the ride that tell riders they’ll be surcharged for repeatedly violating the policy.
The other phone, with its location set to “never” sharing, was able to activate tickets without penalties or warnings — even after two or three stops into a trip after boarding.
The LIRR, which operates as one of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s commuter railroads, didn’t offer an explanation for the discrepancy.
The MTA only pointed to the TrainTime app’s terms of services when confronted with The Post’s findings.
The terms of service and conditions claim that location data is stored entirely separate from each customer’s TrainTime account.
The agency also didn’t respond to questions about what the stored data is used for.
LIRR tickets aren’t associated with a specific train, which experts said showed the app shouldn’t “know” if a user is on board a moving train except if the phone’s location is being used as a giveaway.
The TrainTime app’s vendor, Masabi, a London-based company whose ticketing software runs inside the app, said in its own privacy policy that it handles that rider data only as a processor, leaving the MTA in charge of how it’s used.
The Post has filed Freedom of Information Law requests regarding the TrainTime app and location data and is awaiting a response from the MTA.

articles.title_orig: Kremlin accuses Ukraine of 'terrorist activity' in Baltic after cargo ship drone strike
articles.title_zh: Kremlin accuses Ukraine of 'terrorist activity' in Baltic after cargo ship drone strike
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship
Europe live – latest updates
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Stocks are tumbling. Has the AI bubble finally burst?
articles.title_zh: Stocks are tumbling. Has the AI bubble finally burst?
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a May 2026 ceremony in China. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

Pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and high mortgage rates are a big reason why. The National Association of Realtors says its Pending Home Sales Index dropped 4.7% from September to 63.0. That is 16.7% lower than a year earlier, and it is the second straight month of record-low contract signings. Every major U.S. region lost ground. The 30-year mortgage rate is still high, at 7.18% in our latest reading, so many buyers are waiting. NAR's chief economist thinks October could be the low point if rates have topped out. If you can afford today's payment, a slower contract market can give you more room to negotiate. If you are selling, it points to a sluggish stretch for closings.
Source: National Association of Realtors.
NAR published the October figures on November 18, 2026. The Pending Home Sales Index tracks signed contracts on existing homes, not closings. A home goes pending when the buyer and seller sign, and the sale usually closes in one or two months. That is why this report matters. Today's contracts are an early clue to next month's closed sales.
An index of 100 equals the average level of contract activity in 2001. At 63.0, October's reading sits far below that benchmark. In plain terms, far fewer buyers are signing contracts than we would expect in a typical year.
A 16.7% drop from a year earlier is a big move. It means roughly one in six fewer deals got signed than last October. The 4.7% drop from September shows the slowdown did not stop after September had already set a record low.
The main pressure is still the monthly payment. Mortgage rates spent October at some of their highest levels in three years. Freddie Mac says the 30-year fixed averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.25% a year earlier. That kind of jump raises the payment even if the home price barely moves, and a lot of buyers simply step back.
Here is what that looks like in dollars. On a $300,000 loan, principal and interest at 7.33% run about $2,063 a month. At last year's 6.25% average, the same loan would have been about $1,847 a month. That is a difference of roughly $216 a month, or about $2,600 a year, before taxes and insurance.
Rates have eased a little since then, but not enough to change the story. In our latest report on today's mortgage rates , the 30-year fixed purchase rate is 7.18%. That is 15 basis points below Friday and 9 basis points below last week. On that same $300,000 loan, the payment is about $2,032 a month, or roughly $31 less than October's average. It is better, but still high enough to keep many buyers waiting.
Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist, put it this way: “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out.”
That is a hopeful note, not a promise. Rates have slipped from their recent highs, but they are still expensive. Buyers will need to see payments stay more manageable before contract activity can rebuild.
This was not a one-region story. NAR says pending home sales fell from September and from a year earlier in all four major U.S. regions.
The pattern is familiar. The West, where home prices are often the highest, took the hardest hit. A rate near 7% adds the most dollars to a monthly payment in expensive markets. The Northeast held up best, but it still fell. When every region is down at the same time, the national rate backdrop is usually doing most of the work.
Even in a record-low month, some local markets did better than the national average. Among the 50 largest metro areas, these 10 posted the smallest year-over-year declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com Economics that NAR included in its report:
“Smallest decline” is not the same as a gain. Every one of these markets was still down from a year earlier. Cincinnati came closest to holding steady, at a 4.7% drop, which is much milder than the 16.7% national decline. Several of the more resilient names are Midwestern and Northeastern metros, which also had the milder regional declines. If you are shopping, it still helps to look at local contract activity, not only the U.S. average.
If you can handle today's payment, a record-low contract market can work in your favor. Fewer buyers signing deals often means less competition, more time to think, and more room to ask for a lower price, repairs, or help with closing costs.
Here is a simple way to think about it:
An old saying still fits: date the rate, marry the house. If rates fall later, you may be able to refinance. But you can only do that if you can live with the payment you sign up for today. Use the mortgage calculator below to test the payment on the home you have in mind, then compare that number with fresh lender quotes.
Sellers should plan for a slower close to the year. Yun noted that two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings. Many of the homes that would have closed in November and December needed to go under contract in October. A lot of those contracts did not get signed.
That does not mean you have to give your home away. It does mean pricing and presentation matter more now. A home that is priced right, clean, and ready to show can still sell, because the buyers who are shopping now tend to be serious.
If you do not need to sell this winter, you can wait and watch the next few reports. If you do need to sell, be realistic about the payment buyers are facing and be open to reasonable requests.
Yun raised a bigger question than one month's index. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million,” he said. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”
Both things can be true at the same time. Plenty of people still want to buy. High rates have put the payment out of reach for many of them. If rates have truly topped out, as Yun suggests, October's record low could be the bottom for contract signings in this cycle. If rates jump again, the wait could last longer, and annual existing-home sales could end up at their lowest level since the mid-1990s, just as he warned.
I'll be watching the next pending-sales report, and the path of the 30-year rate, to see which way this breaks. If you are planning a move soon, those two numbers are worth watching. In the meantime, start with a payment you can carry, not a rate you hope to get later.

articles.title_orig: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.title_zh: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s Full Self-Driving software, despite its name, isn’t capable of fully driving itself. But try conveying that nuance to elderly folks, who are buying Teslas with the semi-autonomous feature because they can no longer safely drive themselves.
It’s a trend, Fast Company reports , that Tesla has been happy to play into — and represents yet another pain point as the public gets its hands on a piece of sci-fi-sounding technology.
“The extent to which people are willing to adopt these vehicles, and ways that they’re using them are completely wide open,” Johnathon Ehsani, an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Fast Company . “We know nothing.”
Many older people don’t want to give up driving. It’s an acknowledgement that they’re aging and can’t be independent like they used to be. And given the disastrous state of public transportation in this country, many can’t afford to. Without their kids to chauffeur them, how will they get around?
The answer, for an increasing number, is to buy a Tesla with FSD. Tesla’s marketing, and the rhetoric spewed by its CEO Musk, helps push them that way. Musk often says that the cars can “drive themselves,” while the automaker posts promotional videos of owners drinking an espresso while “driving.” That’s despite the vehicle manuals, unlike the company’s marketing, making it clear that FSD can’t safely drive itself without an operator ready to step in at any moment.
Earlier this year, Tesla’s North America account also endorsed a video about a 71-year-old man who bought a Cybertruck with FSD, because “without it, he would have to rely on someone else to drive for him.” “My eyes are getting bad,” the elderly gentleman says in the video.
Again, it’s literally called “Full Self-Driving” — or should we say “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).” Tesla adopted that parenthetical after being sued by the California DMV for misleading advertising. In reality, the cars require constant supervision in case you have to take over at a moment’s notice, unlike robotaxis offered by companies such as Waymo, which don’t require any local human oversight (they do typically employee remote operators to help them out when they get stuck.)
Besides Musk’s legions of fanboys, old people are the most vulnerable to uncritically accepting sci-fi characterizations of the tech and not understanding its drawbacks.
“They don’t know the limitations of these systems,” Birsen Donmez, an engineering professor at the University of Toronto, told Fast Company .
Targeting elderly people is far from the only example of how Tesla has walked a dangerous line in how it markets its tech. It also started recommending drowsy motorists to let FSD take over their cars.
The consequences can be drastic. Many deaths have been linked to Tesla’s self-driving tech. Just last month, a Tesla running FSD crashed into a police cruiser that was stopped at the scene of a car crash after the driver allegedly fell asleep at the wheel, sending two officers to the hospital with serious injuries.

articles.title_orig: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
articles.title_zh: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
articles.content_orig:
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra , a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer , a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health , including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease , and immune response . Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed .
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan , an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis . Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

articles.title_orig: NYC Citi Bike rides to be capped at $3.65 for members under new deal with Lyft
articles.title_zh: NYC Citi Bike rides to be capped at $3.65 for members under new deal with Lyft
articles.content_orig:
Lyft will cap the Citi Bike member cost of any sub-45-minute e-bike trip at $3.65 starting on Jan. 19, Mayor Mamdani said on Monday, and the bike-share provider has also agreed to freeze member rates through the middle of 2029.
The Citi Bike-loving mayor’s announcement — first reported in the New York Times —comes ahead of a City Council hearing on Citi Bike fees scheduled for Dec. 2. All four bills on the meeting’s agenda would offer discount rides or cap rider fees. Council Speaker Julie Menin is scheduled to appear at the mayor’s Citi Bike announcement on Monday morning.
Lyft made $24 million off the bike-share system last year; Transportation Alternatives’ “Citi Bike Riders Union” campaign calls on the city to cap all e-bike rides at $3. Annual membership, meanwhile, has skyrocketed from $95 in 2013 to $239 today. Citi Bike’s only existing e-bike ride price cap is $5.40 for sub-45-minute trips into or out of Manhattan; a 45-minute e-bike ride not going into or out of Manhattan currently costs $12.15.
The company’s contract to run the city’s bike-share program expires on May 26, 2029, though no competitor could likely come close to meeting the capacity demands of the current Citi Bike system. That gives Lyft significant leverage in negotiations with the city.
Editor’s note: This story initially misreported that the new price cap will apply to e-bike trips into our out of Manhattan; it will apply to all e-bike trips.
